title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
corePattern: Monotonic Increasing Stack for Previous and Next Smaller Element
interviewTips: Ask if heights can be empty, contain zeros, or have up to 1e5 elements and if answer fits 32-bit int.
Trade-off: Brute force O(n^2) is simple but TLE; two-pass stack is clearer, one-pass stack with sentinel is optimal and most expected.
Edge tip: use strict vs non-strict inequality consistently for duplicates and always flush stack with sentinel 0; width is i - stack.top - 1 or i if stack empty.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force
approaches.intuition: For every left bar expand right and keep minimum height, area is minHeight * width. The max over all pairs is the answer.
approaches.theory: Fix left index i, iterate right index j >= i maintaining curMin = min(curMin, heights[j]). Candidate area = curMin * (j-i+1). This enumerates all subarrays as potential rectangles limited by minimum bar. Correct because any maximal rectangle has some interval where height equals minimum.

timeComplexity.explanation: n left positions each expands up to n rights, constant work per pair.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only minH and maxArea variables besides input.

steps: i=0: expand j=0..5, min sequence 2,1,1,1,1,1 -> best 1*6=6
i=3: min 6 -> area 6, overall max stays 10
other i give smaller areas, final answer 10

edgeCases: Strictly decreasing needs full width with smallest bar

approaches.name: Approach 2: Previous and Next Smaller with Monotonic Stack
approaches.intuition: For each bar as the limiting height, find how far it can extend left and right until a smaller bar stops it. Width * height is its best rectangle.
approaches.theory: Compute left[i] = index of previous smaller element and right[i] = index of next smaller element using increasing stack. Pop while stack top >= current to maintain strict smaller boundaries. Then width = right[i]-left[i]-1 and area = heights[i]*width. Each index pushed and popped at most once, so linear. Correct because maximal rectangle for height heights[i] is exactly bounded by first smaller on each side.

timeComplexity.explanation: Two linear passes, each index pushed and popped at most once.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Stack plus left and right arrays of size n.

edgeCases: Duplicates [2,2,2]: use >= to avoid double counting, width spans all
Increasing [1,2,3]: left is i-1, right is n
Decreasing [3,2,1]: left is -1, right is i+1

approaches.name: Approach 3: One-Pass Monotonic Stack with Sentinel
approaches.intuition: Keep increasing stack of bar indices. When a lower bar arrives, all taller bars on stack must end here, so pop and compute their rectangles immediately.
approaches.theory: Stack maintains increasing heights. For current index i with height cur, while stack top height > cur, pop top h. Its right boundary is i (first smaller to right) and left boundary is new stack top (previous smaller). Width = i if stack empty else i - stack.top -1. Area = h*width. Append sentinel 0 to flush remaining stack. Each bar pushed and popped once, giving optimal linear time with single pass.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each bar pushed once and popped once, single scan with sentinel.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Monotonic stack holds at most n indices, worst case increasing heights.

steps: i=0 push 0 (2), i=1: 1<2 pop 0 width=1 area=2 push 1 (1)
i=4 h=2: pop 3 h=6 width=4-2-1=1 area=6, pop 2 h=5 width=4-1-1=2 area=10 push 4
i=5 push 5 (3), i=6 h=0 flush rest max stays 10

edgeCases: Single element [1] with sentinel flushes correctly
Large n=1e5 increasing: stack grows to n but still O(n)
Do not forget sentinel else tallest suffix never popped
